text: A patent is a government-granted exclusive right to an invention, giving the patent holder the right to exclude others from making, using, selling, offering for sale, or importing the patented invention for a limited time (20 years in India from filing date). In exchange, the inventor publicly discloses the invention. Patents can cover products, processes, apparatus, and compositions of matter. For AYUSH, patents may cover novel formulations, extraction processes, drug delivery systems, and manufacturing methods.

Prior art is all information publicly available anywhere in the world before the priority date of a patent application. It includes: patents, publications, products on sale, public demonstrations, oral presentations, websites. Prior art is used to assess novelty and inventive step. If an invention is fully disclosed in prior art, it cannot be patented (lacks novelty). For AYUSH, prior art includes classical Ayurvedic texts, TKDL database, scientific publications, and earlier patents.

Novelty means the invention is new — not anticipated by any single prior art reference. Under Section 2(l) of Patents Act, an invention is new if it has not been: published anywhere before the priority date, publicly used in India, or part of traditional knowledge (TKDL). If every element of a patent claim is found in one prior art document, the claim lacks novelty. For AYUSH: if your exact formulation is in Charaka Samhita, it's not novel.

Inventive step (non-obviousness) means the invention involves a technical advance compared to existing knowledge and is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. Under Section 2(ja) of Patents Act, assessed by: what would a skilled person think when combining prior art? If they would easily arrive at the invention, no inventive step. For AYUSH: even if individual herbs are known, a specific combination with unexpected synergy may have inventive step.

Industrial applicability means the invention can be made or used in some kind of industry. Under Section 2(ac), includes agriculture. This is a low bar — most inventions meet it. Theoretical discoveries without practical application may fail. For AYUSH: a formulation that can be manufactured and used medicinally has industrial applicability. A purely theoretical hypothesis without application doesn't qualify.

Priority date is the earliest filing date from which the patent application claims protection. If filing first in India, priority date = Indian filing date. If claiming priority from foreign application (Paris Convention) or provisional application, priority date = that earlier date. Prior art is assessed against priority date. For AYUSH: file provisional application early to establish priority date, then complete with full data within 12 months.

Specification is the document describing the invention in detail. Contains: Title, Field of invention, Background, Summary, Detailed description, Examples, Claims, Abstract, Drawings (if applicable). Provisional specification: filed with provisional application, less detailed. Complete specification: full disclosure, required for examination. Specification must enable a skilled person to practice the invention. For AYUSH: include formulation details, preparation methods, experimental data.

Claims define the legal scope of the patent — what the patent holder can exclude others from doing. Independent claims stand alone; dependent claims narrow independent claims. Claim interpretation determines infringement. Claims must be: clear, concise, supported by specification. Number of claims affects fees. For AYUSH: claim the formulation, process, dosage forms; use ranges to maximize scope while maintaining validity.

Patent prosecution is the process of obtaining a patent through the Patent Office. Includes: filing, examination, responding to objections (FER), amendments, hearings, grant. Prosecution history (file wrapper) is the record of all interactions with Patent Office. Can be relevant for claim interpretation in infringement cases. For AYUSH: skilled prosecution maximizes claim scope while overcoming examiner objections.

First Examination Report (FER) is the examiner's initial assessment of the patent application. Lists objections: formal defects, novelty issues (prior art cited), lack of inventive step, Section 3 exclusions, unclear claims. Applicant must respond within 6 months (extendable by 3 months). Response addresses each objection with arguments and/or amendments. For AYUSH: FER often raises Section 3(d) and 3(p); respond with data and prior art distinctions.

Opposition is a procedure to challenge patent grant/validity. Pre-grant opposition (Section 25(1)): filed before grant, by any person. Post-grant opposition (Section 25(2)): filed within 1 year of grant, by 'interested person'. Grounds include: lack of novelty, obviousness, non-patentable subject matter, insufficient disclosure. For AYUSH: monitor competitor filings, oppose if threatening; conversely, build strong applications to withstand opposition.

Revocation cancels an already-granted patent. Under Section 64, can be filed: by counterclaim in infringement suit, or by petition to Appellate Board. Grounds same as opposition plus: non-working in India. Section 66: government can revoke in public interest. Revocation is post-grant remedy when opposition period has passed. For AYUSH: defend your patents against revocation; consider revocation of blocking competitor patents.

Provisional application establishes priority date without full disclosure. File with provisional specification when invention concept is ready but full details/data are being developed. Within 12 months, must file complete specification. Advantages: lower fee, secures early date, allows 'Patent Pending' label. If complete spec not filed, application lapses. For AYUSH: file provisional when formulation shows promise; complete after trials.

Convention application claims priority from earlier filing in a Convention country (Paris Convention member). Must file within 12 months of first foreign filing. Benefits from earlier priority date for prior art assessment. Requires filing priority documents. For AYUSH: if filing first abroad, can enter India within 12 months claiming that priority.

PCT (Patent Cooperation Treaty) application is an international filing through WIPO that simplifies multi-country patenting. Single application designates multiple countries. Provides: international search report, preliminary examination. Within 30/31 months, must enter national phase in chosen countries. Not a 'world patent' — just deferred national filing. For AYUSH exporters: PCT enables strategic market selection over 30 months.

Patent agent is a professional registered to practice before the Indian Patent Office. Qualifications: degree in specified technical field + passed patent agent exam. Can: file and prosecute patent applications, conduct searches, provide patentability opinions. Cannot: appear in courts (unlike patent attorneys who are also advocates). For AYUSH: work with patent agents having pharma/biotech expertise for best results.

Assignment is transfer of patent ownership from assignor to assignee. Must be in writing (assignment deed). Recorded with Patent Office. After assignment, assignee is the new patent owner with all rights. Distinguished from licensing which doesn't transfer ownership. For AYUSH: inventors often assign to employer company; verify clean assignment chain for all IP transactions.

License is permission to use a patented invention. Licensor (patent owner) grants rights to licensee. Exclusive license: only licensee can use. Non-exclusive: multiple licensees possible. Terms include: territory, field, royalty, duration. License doesn't transfer ownership. Must be in writing; recordal optional but recommended. For AYUSH: license your patents to partners for markets you can't reach.

Infringement is unauthorized making, using, selling, offering for sale, or importing of a patented invention. Direct infringement: doing prohibited acts. Indirect infringement: contributing to or inducing infringement. Remedies: injunction, damages, account of profits. Defense: patent invalidity, non-infringement, license. For AYUSH: before commercializing, conduct freedom-to-operate analysis to avoid infringing others' patents.

Working statement (Form 27) is an annual declaration of how the patent is being worked in India. Required under Section 146. Due by June 30 each year. Disclose: whether worked, extent of working, reasons if not working, license info. Non-filing penalty: up to Rs 10 lakh. Non-working can trigger compulsory licensing. For AYUSH patentees: maintain production records for accurate Form 27 filing.
